A1.justification: Despite the title change, the shared Chebyshev-based LDS framework and matched derivations establish continuity of the research. Both complete PDFs, including their appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 contains algorithms, theoretical results, analytical examples, and proofs, but no original empirical results in either the main text or appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic experiments on linear dynamics, nonlinear dynamics, and RNN-generated sequences in Section 5, Tables 2–4, and Appendix E.

M1.justification: v2 introduces general offline and online preconditioning wrappers, standalone convolutional preconditioned regression, and a Legendre variant. Its spectral-filtering algorithm also replaces v1's polynomial-weighted filter matrix with an unweighted complex moment matrix and changes the regression parameterization. These are procedural changes beyond renaming.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical dataset coverage. v2 evaluates prediction on synthetic 300-dimensional linear dynamics, 10-dimensional nonlinear dynamics, and sequences generated by a sparse 10-layer LSTM network, including multiple complex-eigenvalue thresholds.

E2.justification: v2 introduces evaluated comparisons against no preconditioning and jointly learned preconditioning coefficients for regression, spectral filtering, and neural predictors. Tables 2–4 establish these comparators' participation; v1 contains no empirical comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 5 introduces length-2000 sequences, Gaussian inputs, specified neural model configurations, and mean absolute error over the final 200 predictions. Learning rates are selected from a three-value grid, with separate model/coefficient rate pairs for learned preconditioning. These are new experimental protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds polynomial-degree sensitivity tests, comparisons across complex-eigenvalue thresholds, and neural-depth analyses using 8-, 9-, and 10-layer predictors. Appendix E examines high-degree deterioration and differences between fixed and learned coefficients. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: v2 first reports results across 200 runs, with mean and standard deviation in Tables 2–4 and captions identifying 200 independent runs for the appendix plots. v1 has no repeated-run or empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 and Figures 2–7 add numerical errors, learning curves, and comparative findings absent from v1. For example, Table 4 reports 0.54 ± 0.23 for the unconditioned predictor and 0.08 ± 0.03 for degree-5 Chebyshev preconditioning. These are newly reported experiments, not version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds the regression theorem and proof, revises the approximation and optimization bounds, and replaces the Hankel-based spectral-decay argument with a quadrature/Krylov argument. v1's T^(17/20) comparator-regret theorem becomes stated cumulative-error bounds of T^(11/13) and T^(10/13), under LDS-generated outputs and eigenvalue-argument restrictions rather than the earlier imaginary-part restriction.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from dimension-free regret for asymmetric LDS via spectral filtering to universal sequence preconditioning across prediction methods, including empirical nonlinear and neural applications. Meanwhile, v1's explicit arbitrary-sequence comparator guarantee is narrowed in v2's formal theorems to LDS-generated outputs.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of truncating versus learning the residual, high-degree degradation, and the learner-dependent benefits of learned coefficients. It also proposes universal preconditioning as an initialization for other learning methods. The explicit discussion of the unresolved upper/lower learnability-bound gap in v1's conclusion is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial experimental documentation: generator equations and dimensions, neural depths and widths, polynomial degrees, learning-rate grids, and evaluation procedures. These details were absent from v1. Reproducibility remains incomplete because parameters such as spectral-radius limits and noise variance are left symbolic.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around generalizing classical differencing and ARIMA-style preprocessing, adding Box and Jenkins and connections to universal and learned optimizers. It also adds quadrature-related positioning for the revised proof. Much of v1's LDS/control survey is retained in Appendix A.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around universal preconditioning. Existing related work, memory-capacity discussion, and proof material move into reorganized appendices, while the main text separates algorithms, significance, analysis, and experiments.

P2.justification: v2 expands one algorithm display into four, adds a method-capability table, three experimental tables, a geometric proof illustration, and six multipanel experimental figures. It also adds a contents page and changes headers, pagination placement, and equation layout.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the preconditioning idea more operational and supplies controlled, repeated-run evidence showing where it helps and fails. These improve practical understanding. However, the faster theoretical rates use narrower assumptions, and Section 1.1's broad superiority claim over learned preconditioning exceeds the mixed evidence in Tables 2–3. The net quality gain is therefore limited despite the substantial revision.
